title: The Savoy Male and Female College
text:
Mr. Hunt is the only surviving member of the regular College faculty of the Savoy College.


ELBU BENNETT HINSHAW

Elbu B. Hinshaw, who came to the Savoy College faculty early in 1887 to fill the vacancy in classical languages when Professor Holland retired, was of Pennsylvania Quaker ancestry, the son of Jacob and Elizabeth (Barker) Hinshaw of the Keystone State. Elbu Bennett Hinshaw was born October 14, 1860, in Indiana. Indian. The following account from D. C. Gideon's History of the Indian Territory gives a picture of Mr. Hinshaw's training and abilities during the last three years of Savoy College:

Professor Hinshaw, of this review, completed his education in Hiwasee College, in Tennessee, where he was graduated in 1884 with the degree of Bachelor of Science. Since then the degree of Master of Arts has been conferred upon him by his alma mater, which is one of the oldest institutions of learning in the mountain sections of the middle South. After his graduation Professor Hinshaw entered upon the work of instruction, having taken charge of a high school in East Tennessee for two years, after which he became connected with Savoy College in Grayson County, Texas. For five years work there becoming known, in 1887 he was selected to accept the position of president of the Bloomfield Seminary in Panola County, in the Chickasaw Nation. He accepted this and has been in continuous service in this institution for some twenty years. Bloomfield Seminary is an educational institution established by the Chickasaw government for the education of the young Indian women and the children of new citizens. It was established before the war at its present location in Chickasaw Nation, and has been in existence for fifty years. . . . The number of pupils in attendance is two hundred and twenty, including all departments, and the list of applicants is very large in number, so many being desirous of entering the institution. . . .
